opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something we think about constantly, because the worst thing you can do right now is build a product that's perfectly tuned to the limitations of today's models. Those limitations change every few months, and if your whole architecture is built around working around them, you end up with a lot of scaffolding that becomes dead weight, or even actively gets in the way, once the next generation comes out.

So our basic philosophy is to ask: what would we want this tool to look like if the model were dramatically smarter than it is today? Then we work backwards from that. In practice that means we try not to over-constrain the model. We avoid hard-coding long, rigid pipelines where the model is just filling in blanks at each step. We'd rather give it good tools, good context, and a clear sense of the goal, and let it decide how to get there. Today that sometimes means it takes a wrong turn and we have to catch it. But every time a new model drops, the product gets better almost for free, instead of us having to rip things out.

The other piece is that a lot of the durable value isn't in the clever prompting. It's in the stuff around the model that stays useful no matter how capable it gets. That's things like the environment it operates in, access to the right data and compute, the ability to run experiments and check its own work, and good interfaces for a human researcher to see what's going on, steer it, and trust the results. A smarter model doesn't make those less important. If anything it makes them more important, because you're going to hand it longer, more ambitious tasks, and you need visibility and verification to match.

We also try to be honest with ourselves about which features are crutches. If something exists only because the current model is bad at X, we mark it mentally as temporary, and we revisit it with every model release. Some of those get deleted, and that's a good day.

And finally, we build a lot of internal evals around the kinds of research tasks we actually care about. When a new model comes out, we can quickly see where the frontier has moved and what that unlocks. Often the most exciting moment is realizing that a task that was totally out of reach six months ago is now something the model can just do, and then the question becomes how fast we can reshape the product to let users take advantage of it.

r001.rationale: The response advocates designing the tool for smarter future models and giving models tools and context, but does not say a well-designed harness lets current models preview next-generation capabilities.

r002.rationale: It describes new models unlocking previously out-of-reach tasks, but does not state that each model generation has substantial capabilities that remain untapped.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is honestly the question we spend the most time on, because the thing you're building for isn't the model that exists today, it's the one that's going to exist in six or twelve months, and if you design too tightly around current limitations you've basically built a product with an expiration date.

The way I think about it is, there's a distinction between scaffolding that compensates for a weakness and scaffolding that reflects the actual structure of the problem. A lot of what people build right now is the first kind. The model can't hold enough context, so you chunk things up a certain way. The model forgets what it was doing, so you add a bunch of checkpoints and state management. The model hallucinates a citation, so you bolt on a verification step. Those are reasonable things to do today, but every one of them is a bet that the weakness persists, and historically those bets have lost. The bitter lesson stuff applies here too. The more you encode your own clever workarounds, the more you get steamrolled when the next model just doesn't need them.

So with Silico, we try to ask, what would this look like if the model were a genuinely good scientist? Not a good autocomplete, a good scientist. And a good scientist still needs things. They need access to data. They need the ability to run an experiment and see what happens. They need to be able to go back and look at what they tried before. They need a way to communicate findings to a human who's going to make decisions based on them. None of that goes away when the model gets smarter. If anything it matters more, because a more capable model that can't actually touch the world is just a more expensive way to generate plausible-sounding papers.

The other piece is that we try to keep the human in a role that scales. Right now the human is often doing a lot of correction, like catching the model when it goes off the rails. That's a role that shrinks as models improve, and if your whole interface is built around correction, your product gets less useful as the models get better, which is a bizarre place to be. So we try to orient the human's role toward direction and judgment. What questions matter, what's actually interesting, what do we believe and why. Those are the things that stay valuable.

And then, candidly, we try to be a little humble about it. We don't actually know the shape of what's coming. So we build things to be swappable, we try not to overfit the architecture to any one lab's quirks, and when a new model comes out, the first thing we do is rip out a bunch of scaffolding and see what breaks. Usually less than we expect. That's been one of the more consistent findings, that the thing we thought we needed, we often didn't.

r001.rationale: The response discusses designing Silico for future models and removing workarounds, but does not say a well-designed harness lets current models preview next-generation capabilities.

r002.rationale: The response says models may not need as much scaffolding as expected, but does not state that each model generation has substantial untapped capabilities.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is, you want to build for where the models are going, while still making something useful with the models you have today. That means being careful about which parts of the product are compensating for a temporary limitation and which parts will remain valuable as the models improve.

For a research tool, the enduring value is helping someone move from a question to an answer they can actually trust. Can the system find the relevant information, connect it to the question, and make the evidence easy to inspect? More capable models should make that experience better, and let us hand off more of the process without losing that visibility.

So I’d want the architecture to give us room to do that. You don’t want to bake today’s model limitations so deeply into the workflow that a better model comes along and you have to rebuild everything. You want to be able to try it, see where it succeeds, and expand what the system can do based on that evidence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to build for where the models are going, while still making something useful with the models we have today. You don’t want to spend all your time engineering around a limitation that disappears with the next release. But you also can’t just assume that a smarter model will automatically make a great research tool.

For Silico, that means keeping the underlying models fairly interchangeable and focusing on the research workflow: What context does the system need? What tools can it use? How can someone inspect the evidence behind an answer and steer the next step? Those things still matter as the models improve.

And then you want to keep testing your assumptions. When a new model comes out, can you give it a larger piece of the task? Can you remove some scaffolding? Ideally, better models let us make the product simpler while letting researchers tackle more ambitious questions.
